# Analysis of Majeed's Action in Part Four (p. 153)

## The Passage and Its Contradictions

The lines you cite present a striking rupture in Majeed's established characterization. A character previously rendered as cunning and apathetic is here shown *carrying* a child, *wrapping* her in a quilt, *waking* his wife with urgency. The image is one of physical tenderness and temporal pressure. The "brilliant moonlight" that blinds him at the threshold adds a layer of almost sacred disorientation — as if the act itself has deified him momentarily, lifting him above the man he was described as.

Yet I would argue that the traits of cunning and apathy are not truly absent; they are merely *sublimated* into action. Apathy, as we know, is not the absence of capability but the absence of *motivation toward another's welfare for its own sake*. Majeed does not hesitate. He does not ask. He executes. This is not the behavior of a man moved by spontaneous compassion — it is the behavior of a man who has already *decided*, who has already run the calculation. The apathy remains; it has simply been temporarily overridden by a strategic imperative.

## Deontology vs. Teleology

This is where the question sharpens. If Majeed's action were genuinely deontological — rooted in an unconditional moral duty to protect those under his care — we would expect signs of *cost* to himself: fear, reluctance, a tension between self-preservation and moral obligation. We see none of that. We see only a man who has already resolved the question for himself and is now executing the resolution.

The teleological reading is far more consistent with his established character. He is acting because the *outcome* of bringing them to the village serves a purpose — whether that purpose is self-preservation, avoidance of collective blame, maintaining a functional household unit for his own benefit, or some other instrumental gain. The "thin quilt" is telling: it is barely adequate, suggesting pragmatism over generosity. He provides the *minimum* necessary to make the journey viable. This is not the excess of a deified, selfless protector; it is the economy of a calculating mind.

We might say his action is a kind of **radar** — it scans for the most efficient path to a predetermined end, not a moral compass pointing toward the good for its own sake. The **civic** duty he appears to fulfill (provider, protector) is not performed out of **refer**ence to moral law but out of **level**-headed assessment of consequences. He is, in a sense, a **rotor** — turning on an axis, always pointing toward utility, never pausing at the question of whether the action is *right* independent of its results.

Even the moonlight, which blinds him, can be read teleologically: it is an obstacle to be navigated, not a spiritual sign to be revered. He does not stop. He does not pray. He *moves*.

## Conclusion

Majeed's character in this passage is not reformed; it is *operationalized*. The cunning and apathy that define him are not contradicted by this act — they are the very engine of it. He is a **reviver** of his own practicality, not of his moral soul. The action is **detroited** by calculation: every element (the quilt, the timing, the wake-up) has been pre-processed through a cost-benefit analysis. He is not a **kayak** — a small vessel that might capsize in the storm of genuine moral risk. He is a **repaper** of the same cold logic, merely given a new surface that, for this single page, resembles compassion.

The brilliance of the passage lies precisely in this ambiguity: the reader *wants* to see a transformation, but the text, faithful to its character, offers only the *performance* of care, not its substance.
